31 July 2026

Who’d be a telco? Or more specifically, who’d be Optus? This week you have your chance to buy the problem-plagued company.

Also, a federal Court judge slaps to government for its poor understanding of AI, and Elon Musk continues to have a sook about All the Things.

Singtel has confirmed it’s in talks to sell its stake in Optus. I wonder why. In definitely unrelated news, ACMA is suing Optus over last year’s 13-hour outage which included a claimed 1,005 Triple Zero failures.

“Giving access to the emergency call service is not optional, it is a fundamental legal obligation and the most important public safety responsibility telecommunications providers have,” says ACMA chair Nerida O’Loughlin.

Optus has already paid a $12 million penalty for a previous failure.

This time the penalty could be up to $250,000 per instance, and each failure involves two penalty possibilities, failing to give customers access to emergency call services, and failing to ensure those calls were properly transferred. So all that could come to more than $500 million in fines ($).

Meanwhile Optus still faces potential penalties from its massive data breach in 2022. In the ongoing class action being led by law firm Slater and Gordon, the Federal Court has set a trial date of 7 June 2027.

What happens next for Optus is now in the hands of the corporate powerbrokers in Singapore.

This afternoon I was reminded that Singtel has probably been thinking of selling Optus since that 2022 data breach. Presumably no one has been interested. There’s a rumour mill that they’re currently trying to sell a one-third share for $2 billion, but I’m not sure what kind of dollars, AU or SG or US. And yes that’s just a rumour.

In the Federal Court case of Prygodicz v Commonwealth of Australia (Robodebt settlement), Justice Jonathan Beach’s judgment published this week has a stern warning for government ministers and public servants: to “properly inform themselves” about AI and automated systems more generally.

The CEOs and board members of businesses and other organisations might also take note.

I’m republishing the relevant six paragraphs here in full. Not only are they a powerful message, they’re also an excellent example of the restrained judicial language of rebuke.

•••

This Robodebt debacle is something that we have to learn the lessons from or should I say Commonwealth ministers and their departments have to learn the lessons from.

Surely ministers must properly inform themselves of the technical and legal complexities of automated systems and schemes to which members of the public are to be subjected. Such a motivation and skill set are not optional extras. Further, the concept of being a responsible minister does not mean finding a public servant to take responsibility for the policy that you have sought to push through. And nor is the role of a minister simply to educate yourself about the policy through a one page document. And nor is the intellectual exercise simply limited to following the instruction on a “post it” note, which tells you where to place your signature on the executive minute.

Now when dealing with automated processes and systems, any moral hazard problem becomes magnified. If you have not conscientiously and diligently taken steps to either master the detail yourself, or made sure that others reporting to you have done so, you are likely as in this case to inflict real harm on others in imposing automated systems or processes. And as in this case, the relevant ministers and their departments had the freedom and control to take great risks with Robodebt and its implementation, yet they were insulated and detached from the consequences of such risks if they came to fruition, which they obviously did.

Now why am I making these points? Robodebt is over as a system or process, although not of course for the victims and their families, many of whom are still suffering significantly in its aftermath, and some whose spirit only remains in our memory.

Today we of course have generative artificial intelligence. And we will later move into artificial general intelligence. The benefits and rewards of such systems will be several orders of magnitude above the types of automated systems that we have seen in the past. But the complexity and risks of such systems and processes will be equally if not more magnified or amplified.

Surely the lessons learnt from Robodebt can be put to good advantage, not for the technology as such which is morally neutral, but for its human designers, implementers and controllers.

•••

Thanks to the Guardian’s Josh Taylor for bringing this to our attention.
